title: Can We Inspire a Love of Reading?
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos argues that teachers cannot reliably manufacture a love of reading and should prioritise teaching children to read well. She challenges the Balanced Literacy slogan about inspiring lifelong love of reading, citing Dehaene and Goldenberg on the non-negotiable role of decoding. Drawing on Harris, Pinker and Caplan, she contends that personality and interest shape reading preferences far more than teacher inspiration, illustrating with her own reading history and her two sons. She charges that the romance of loving reading has led some teachers to skimp on systematic phonics. Her conclusion is that proficient reading, beginning reading instruction and knowledge-building must take precedence, leaving students to discover for themselves whether they love it.
points: Teaching the code is the primary, objective goal; love of reading is subjective, variable and secondary.
Dehaene and Goldenberg are used to show that mapping symbols to sounds is non-negotiable for all readers.
Personality and personal interest shape reading preferences more than teacher inspiration, so mismatched material can breed resistance.
The pursuit of a romantic ideal can lead teachers to avoid explicit phonics instruction and waste the early window for teaching it.
Choosing book quality (character, theme, language, plot) is negotiable, but guaranteeing love is beyond a teacher's control.
quotes: Here’s what some Whole Language and Balanced Literacy advocates have backwards: They often claim that every child learns to read differently but also contend that there is enough uniformity within our students for us to be able to inspire a lifelong love of reading in all of them. In fact, both of these propositions are problematic.

Yes, we immerse our students in authentic literature and attempt to inspire them to become lifelong readers, but this is secondary to the primary goal of something far more objective: giving them the tools to access print at any age. If love blossoms en route, so much the better—and we celebrate it without automatically anticipating it.
Like the horse to water, we can lead our students to literature, but we can’t make them love it. And that’s okay. Children are not blank slates when it comes to desires.

Anything that smacks of drudgery—like mastering phonics—might deter us from becoming a lifelong reader, these Balanced Literacy teachers theorize; hence, their avoidance behaviors when it comes to systematic and explicit instruction of foundational skills. Why not, they imply, simply dismiss the drudge of decoding and rush headlong into making meaning?

We have got to do a better job teaching beginning reading, building knowledge, and bridging reading with writing. These challenges must take precedence over inspiring a lifelong love of reading, as admirable as that goal may be.

You can't teach kids to love reading. You can only teach them how to read well enough so they can discover for themselves if they love doing it. Either way, the skill that develops will last a lifetime.
